case_analysis.focal_point: Whether New Jersey Transit Corporation qualifies as an “arm of the State” such that it is entitled to interstate (and Eleventh Amendment–type) sovereign immunity from private suits in another State’s courts, and how courts should weigh financial liability versus other indicia of state control in that determination.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Constitution—state sovereign immunity doctrine (including Eleventh Amendment principles as applied through the Court’s broader state sovereign immunity jurisprudence) and the “arm-of-the-state” test; related state-law backdrop: New Jersey Tort Claims Act, N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 59:1-1 to 59:12-3 (raised in discussion of waiver/consent).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Galette (and similarly situated plaintiffs in the parallel case) argues that NJ Transit should not be treated as the State itself for sovereign-immunity purposes because it functions like a separate, state-created transportation enterprise rather than a core state governmental unit; the analysis should not be dominated by the State’s asserted exposure to paying judgments, and factors such as the State’s own statutory/structural characterization of NJ Transit, its operational and corporate separateness, and how comparable public authorities are treated should weigh against extending sovereign immunity.
case_analysis.respondent_position: NJ Transit/New Jersey argues that NJ Transit is an arm of the State and thus enjoys sovereign immunity in out-of-state or federal-style immunity analyses; in determining arm-of-the-state status, the State’s formal legal responsibility for NJ Transit’s debts or judgments (and the resulting impact on the state treasury) should carry especially heavy—potentially dispositive—weight, and NJ Transit’s statutory structure and relationship to the State demonstrate sufficient state control and integration to warrant immunity.
key_precedents: Infinity Broad. Corp. v. N.J. Meadowlands Comm’n, 901 A.2d 312 (N.J. 2006)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s concern that “treasury risk” could become a free-floating proxy for immunity is the best argument for Petitioner, but it does not describe how the inquiry operates on this record. As Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, fisc is not doing the work alone; it is one practical indicator—considered with pervasive state control and statutory characterization—that the suit is, in substance, against New Jersey itself. Properly framed, this is an arm-of-the-State/real-party-in-interest question rooted in the plan of the Convention, not a waiver or abrogation case, so we should not infer exposure to sister-State private damages suits absent unmistakably clear consent. A narrow holding limited to entities with this degree of integration and realistic fiscal and governance consequences should answer Justice Jackson’s overbreadth worry while remaining faithful to Hyatt and our arm-of-the-State precedents.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s best point is that “practical” treasury exposure and political pressure should not substitute for a legal obligation to pay, lest we collapse corporate separateness into an immunity trump. But the interstate-immunity rule is structural, rooted in the Constitution’s original design: the question is whether the forum State is, in substance, subjecting another State to private coercive process through its alter ego, and fisc consequences are probative of that sovereign indignity even when not reduced to a formal indemnity. As the Chief Justice notes, New Jersey’s creation, characterization, and pervasive control of NJ Transit to perform an essential statewide governmental function—together with realistic fiscal and governance impacts—make this litigation functionally one against New Jersey itself. And absent unmistakably clear consent by New Jersey to be haled into a sister-State court for private damages suits, I see no constitutional basis to deny immunity here consistent with Alden and Hyatt.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s strongest point is that we should not let an amorphous notion of “treasury risk” swallow the arm-of-the-State inquiry when the State has chosen a corporately separate vehicle. But as the Chief Justice explains, the fisc factor here is not a free-floating presumption; it is evidence—alongside pervasive state control and statutory characterization—of whether the forum State’s coercive process would, in substance, operate against New Jersey itself through an alter ego. That structural intrusion is the core federalism harm Hyatt sought to prevent, and it is not cured by pointing to formal separateness if, in practical operation, the entity is tightly integrated into state governance and financially dependent on state support. And as Justice Kagan notes, nothing in New Jersey law supplies the unmistakably clear consent required to subject the State (or its true instrumentality) to private damages suits in another State’s courts.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Jackson is right to caution against letting an amorphous “practical exposure” concept become a categorical treasury-risk trigger that overrides statutory separateness; our arm-of-the-State inquiry must remain a structured, doctrine-bound assessment of whether the State is the real party in interest. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, the fisc point here is not free-floating: it corroborates pervasive state control, statutory characterization as a public instrumentality, and integration into statewide governance such that the suit would, in substance, operate against New Jersey itself. On that record, this is an alter-ego case under Hess/Regents, not a mere corporate-form case, and New Jersey has not supplied the unequivocal, unmistakably clear consent necessary to subject the State (or its arm) to private damages actions in a sister-State court. Recognizing interstate sovereign immunity here applies—not dilutes—the doctrine’s prerequisites and preserves the baseline rule absent a clear waiver.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Jackson is right to resist any arm-of-the-State rule that turns on a free-floating, near-dispositive “treasury risk” divorced from law; corporate form and statutory design can matter, and Hess cautions against simplistic proxies. But as the Chief Justice explains, the fisc point here is not a talisman—it is one indicator, alongside pervasive state control and the State’s own characterization of the entity as an instrumentality performing statewide governmental functions, that the suit is in substance against New Jersey itself. Given that structural premise, the waiver question is straightforward: as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, nothing in New Jersey’s tort-claims regime provides the unmistakably clear consent required to subject the State (or its alter ego) to private damages actions in a sister State’s courts. Under our doctrine treating sovereign immunity as a constitutional presupposition “absent consent,” extending interstate immunity on these facts follows, rather than evades, Alden/Hyatt and the arm-of-the-State line of cases.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s best point is that we should not let “practical” treasury exposure alone erase statutory corporate separateness, and she is right to insist that legal responsibility matters. But as the Chief explains, our arm-of-the-State cases do not elevate any single factor into a trump; they ask whether the suit is, in substance, one “against” the State, and here pervasive state control and statutory integration make the coercive process operate on New Jersey through its instrumentality even if formal liability is indirect. Justice Kagan’s emphasis that nothing in the New Jersey Tort Claims Act supplies the unmistakably clear consent needed to subject the State (or its alter ego) to private damages suits in a sister-State court reinforces that this is not a place for implied surrender. Given Hyatt/Alden’s structural premise and the absence of clear waiver, I would treat NJ Transit as an arm of the State on this record.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s strongest point is that we should not let “treasury risk” operate as a free-floating trump that disregards statutory separateness and the State’s formal legal obligation to pay. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, our inquiry under Hess and Regents is functional: whether the suit is, in practical effect, against the State given the entity’s characterization, control, and the realistic fiscal and governance consequences of an adverse judgment. On this record, those indicia converge strongly enough that treating NJ Transit as New Jersey’s alter ego better fits the plan-of-the-Convention principle recognized in Hyatt, and it avoids inferring a surrender of interstate immunity absent unmistakably clear consent. I also agree with Justice Barrett that we can and should cabin the holding to entities with this level of integration and practical exposure, leaving genuinely independent, fiscally insulated authorities for another day.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s strongest point is that “treasury risk” should not become a talisman that collapses the arm-of-the-State inquiry into a single, practical-effects factor absent clear legal responsibility. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the fisc inquiry here is not free-floating; it operates alongside pervasive state control and statutory characterization to answer the core structural question whether this suit is, in substance, one that would hale New Jersey itself into another sovereign’s courts. On this record, the entity’s integration into state governance makes the risk of coercive process against the State realistic rather than speculative, and nothing in New Jersey law provides the unmistakably clear consent required to subject the State (or its alter ego) to private damages actions in sister-State courts. Given Hyatt and Alden’s plan-of-the-Convention framework, I see no text-, structure-, or history-based basis to carve out an exception here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take the Chief Justice’s point that, as he frames it, this is an arm-of-the-State question in which control and fiscal exposure help identify whether the suit is “in substance” against New Jersey. But I do not think the “practical consequences” emphasis pressed by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan supplies a principled stopping point unless the State’s law makes the treasury legally answerable for judgments or otherwise collapses the entity’s distinct liabilities; absent that, we risk converting an effects-based intuition into an implied presumption that corporate separateness cannot overcome. Our precedents (including Hess and Regents) treat the fisc inquiry as important, but not as a substitute for identifying legal responsibility and structural separateness in the entity’s design. On this record, I do not see the unmistakably clear showing—either of legal state liability or of New Jersey’s consent to sister-State damages suits—that would justify treating NJ Transit as identical to the State for interstate-immunity purposes.

John Roberts.reasoning: The threshold question is properly classified as whether NJ Transit is the State’s alter ego for purposes of the States’ retained sovereign immunity in the plan of the Convention, not a waiver or abrogation inquiry (so any purported consent under the New Jersey Tort Claims Act would require unmistakably clear language to extend to private suits in sister-State courts). On the specific statutory and structural facts here—NJ Transit’s creation by state law to perform a statewide governmental transportation function, substantial state control over its governance and operations, and the State’s practical exposure if judgments impair the entity’s finances—the indicia of State dignity and accountability align NJ Transit more closely with the State than with a mere political subdivision. Consistent with our arm-of-the-State cases, treasury risk remains a central consideration because it reflects whether the suit is in substance against the State, but it is assessed alongside control and characterization; here, those factors converge rather than point in opposite directions. Because the record points to NJ Transit operating as a state instrumentality integrated into New Jersey’s governmental structure, it should be treated as an arm of the State entitled to interstate sovereign immunity absent an unmistakably clear waiver.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: State sovereign immunity is a structural rule inhering in the Constitution’s original design, and a nonconsenting State may not be subjected to the indignity of private coercive process in another State’s courts absent a clear surrender of immunity. On these facts, New Jersey Transit is sufficiently integrated into New Jersey’s governmental structure—created by state law to perform an essential statewide transportation function and subject to substantial state direction—that treating it as the State’s alter ego best reflects the States’ retained immunity and dignity interests. Consistent with our arm-of-the-State jurisprudence, the State’s practical exposure to judgments (and the consequent threat to the State’s fiscal integrity and leverage over state policy) is a weighty indicator that the suit is, in substance, against New Jersey itself. Nothing in the record suggests New Jersey clearly consented to be haled into another sovereign’s courts for private damages actions merely by establishing NJ Transit or by general tort-claims legislation.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under Hyatt, a State’s immunity from private suit in another State’s courts is a structural, federalism-based limit on the forum State’s judicial power, and that limit would be unlawfully evaded if a State could be haled into sister-state court simply by conducting essential governmental functions through a state-created transportation instrumentality that the State controls. Applying the arm-of-the-State inquiry with an emphasis on clear, administrable boundaries, the most constitutionally salient factor is whether the judgment, in practical effect, operates against the State itself—particularly through exposure of the state fisc or the State’s legally committed resources—because that is what makes the suit an intrusion on a coequal sovereign. Here, New Jersey has integrated NJ Transit into its governmental structure and oversight to provide a core public transportation function, and the risk that judgments will be paid with or backed by state resources (directly or as a practical necessity) counsels treating NJ Transit as the State for interstate-immunity purposes. A multi-factor test that deemphasizes fiscal exposure in favor of malleable “corporate separateness” invites the very ad hoc, nonuniform outcomes that generate tension among sovereigns and uncertainty about when one State may subject another’s operations to its courts.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: State sovereign immunity is the baseline, and the question is whether NJ Transit is so closely tied to New Jersey that it should be treated as the State itself for immunity purposes—a federal-law determination informed by how state law structures and controls the entity. Under Hess and Regents, the inquiry is practical and centered on the relationship between the State and its creation, with particular emphasis on whether an adverse judgment would, in effect, implicate the State’s fisc and dignity rather than merely a separate corporate enterprise. Here, New Jersey’s statutory design and executive control over NJ Transit, together with the State’s asserted exposure to judgments (even if mediated through appropriations or indemnification practices), align NJ Transit more with an arm of the State than with a politically independent public authority. Because plaintiffs point to no unequivocal consent by New Jersey to be haled into another State’s courts for these claims, the arm-of-the-state factors cut in favor of recognizing NJ Transit’s immunity.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Our sovereign-immunity cases treat the States’ nonamenability to private suit as a structural presupposition of the Constitution, and that protection extends to entities that function as the State itself rather than as mere political subdivisions or commercially oriented corporations. Under Hess and Mt. Healthy, the arm-of-the-State inquiry is multi-factor, but the “most salient” consideration is whether a judgment would in practical effect implicate the State treasury and whether the State has structured the entity so that it remains financially and politically accountable to the State. On this record—where New Jersey has intertwined NJ Transit’s fiscal relationship with the State and maintained substantial control over its governance and operations—the better reading of our precedents is that NJ Transit operates as an arm of the State for immunity purposes, and nothing in the New Jersey Tort Claims Act amounts to the clear, express consent required to waive that immunity in another State’s courts. Extending immunity here thus follows, rather than narrows, the Court’s settled rule that absent consent a State (and its true instrumentalities) may not be haled into private damages suits.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Constitution’s structure, as reaffirmed in Hyatt III and Alden, recognizes a State’s immunity from private suits in another State’s courts, and that protection extends to entities that are truly the State’s alter ego rather than a merely state-created corporation. On this record, NJ Transit is statutorily integrated into New Jersey’s government and subject to substantial state direction (including board-level state control and operation as a public instrumentality), making it the kind of entity whose suit is, in practical and legal effect, a suit “against” the State itself. While exposure of the state treasury is not the only relevant indicator, it remains a central one because sovereign immunity’s core purpose is to prevent compelled diversion of public fisc and policy through litigation; New Jersey’s legal backdrop (including its Tort Claims Act framework) underscores that the State has treated NJ Transit’s liabilities as public liabilities subject to sovereign constraints rather than as purely private corporate debts. Absent a clear, unequivocal waiver by New Jersey or a clear statement authorizing suits against the State’s alter ego, the courts of another State may not entertain this action against NJ Transit as an arm of New Jersey.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Arm-of-the-State status is a federal question, but it turns heavily on the State’s own law defining the entity’s character and the practical relationship between New Jersey and NJ Transit. Under Hess and Regents, the most important consideration is whether the State treasury is legally or functionally on the hook for judgments, and the record here—as reflected in New Jersey’s statutory integration and treatment of NJ Transit within the State’s governmental structure—points to substantial state control and a realistic risk that liabilities will implicate the State fisc. Consistent with the sovereignty-preserving clear-statement background principle, we should not presume that New Jersey surrendered its immunity by operating essential transportation services through a state-created instrumentality absent a clear indication to the contrary, and we can limit the holding to entities like NJ Transit that are tightly integrated into state governance and financing. Because the fisc-and-control indicators here align with treating NJ Transit as an arm of the State, it is entitled to interstate sovereign immunity from private suits in another State’s courts.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: A straightforward application of our sovereign-immunity precedent requires asking whether New Jersey Transit is, in substance, the State itself—because haling it into an out-of-state court would subject New Jersey to coercive judicial process if NJ Transit is an arm of the State. Under Hess and Regents, the most salient consideration is the State’s legal obligation for the entity’s liabilities: if the State treasury is legally on the hook for judgments, that strongly indicates arm-of-the-State status; and where the structural and control indicia point in the same direction (state-created entity, substantial state oversight and integration), immunity follows. On this record, New Jersey’s pervasive statutory control over NJ Transit and the practical risk that judgments will be satisfied through state-controlled public funds outweighs plaintiffs’ emphasis on corporate separateness, which cannot by itself defeat immunity where the entity functions as an instrumentality of the State. Absent concrete textual or structural evidence that New Jersey intended to expose this instrumentality to private damages actions in sister-state courts, we should treat it as an arm of the State entitled to sovereign immunity.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The sovereign-immunity inquiry turns on whether, in text, structure, and practical operation, NJ Transit is the State itself; that determination cannot rest on an implied, dispositive “treasury risk” rule untethered to the entity’s actual statutory design and day-to-day separateness. Under the arm-of-the-state framework, the most probative considerations are the State’s legal obligation to satisfy judgments and the degree to which the entity is structured to operate as an independent corporate instrumentality with its own liabilities—features that, here, appear to point away from treating NJ Transit as identical to New Jersey for all suits in another State’s courts. Consistent with a claim- and entity-specific approach to immunity (rather than an automatic extension of the State’s dignity interests to any state-created authority), the record as framed suggests NJ Transit’s corporate separateness and operational independence should carry substantial weight alongside (and not be eclipsed by) asserted fiscal exposure. Because the relevant doctrine requires a close, precedent-by-analogy assessment rather than a categorical presumption of immunity for public authorities, I would not extend interstate sovereign immunity on these facts absent a clearer showing that New Jersey is legally on the hook for NJ Transit’s judgments in a way that makes the suit functionally one against the State.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether New Jersey Transit Corporation qualifies as an “arm of the State” entitled to interstate/Eleventh-Amendment-type sovereign immunity from private suits in another State’s (or federal) courts, and how much weight courts must give to the State’s formal fiscal responsibility for judgments versus other arm-of-the-state factors.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Constitution—state sovereign immunity as reflected in the Eleventh Amendment and the broader structural doctrine of state sovereign immunity (including interstate sovereign immunity recognized in cases like Franchise Tax Bd. v. Hyatt); related to state-law waivers such as the New Jersey Tort Claims Act (N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 59:1-1 to 59:12-3) insofar as waiver/consent is argued.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Galette (and the Colt/Tsai respondents aligned against NJ Transit in the companion case) argue that NJ Transit is not an arm of New Jersey for sovereign-immunity purposes because it operates more like a commercially oriented, state-created transportation enterprise than a core state agency. They contend that the arm-of-the-state inquiry must remain multi-factor and functional, not dominated by a single consideration such as whether the State is formally on the hook for judgments. They also resist arguments that New Jersey’s internal labels or selective invocations of immunity should control, and they dispute that any purported state-law immunity framework (or state characterization) automatically translates into constitutional sovereign immunity in sister-state courts.
case_analysis.respondent_position: NJ Transit and New Jersey argue that NJ Transit is an arm of the State and thus shares New Jersey’s sovereign immunity, including against suits brought outside New Jersey. They emphasize that the State’s treasury risk/formal legal liability for judgments is the most important (or dispositive) factor in the arm-of-the-state test, and that New Jersey law and institutional design treat NJ Transit as part of state government rather than as an independent municipal-style entity. They also argue that there is no clear waiver of sovereign immunity here (rejecting theories of implied or “constructive” consent), and that state-law tort-claims provisions do not amount to consent to be sued in other jurisdictions.
key_precedents: Infinity Broad. Corp. v. N.J. Meadowlands Comm’n, 901 A.2d 312 (N.J. 2006)

John Roberts.reasoning: Properly framed, this case is not about a free-floating “commercial activity” exception to sovereign immunity; it is whether NJ Transit is so identified with New Jersey that a private damages action in a sister-State court is, in substance, a suit against the State itself. The petitioner’s strongest point—separate corporate form and fare-charging operations—cannot overcome the core indicia our cases use to identify the real party in interest, chiefly the State’s legal and practical responsibility for judgments and its pervasive control, as Justice Kagan and Justice Alito emphasized by reference to Hess. Nor does New Jersey’s Tort Claims Act supply the unmistakably clear, forum-specific consent needed to expose the State (or its alter ego) to private suit in another sovereign’s courts; at most it authorizes limited in-state litigation. Accepting petitioner’s reframing would invite ad hoc relabeling of state instrumentalities as “commercial” and erode the structural immunity Hyatt and Alden recognize.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest contention—that NJ Transit’s corporate form and fare-charging, “commercial” operations defeat immunity—mistakes labels for the Constitution’s structural design. As the Chief Justice and Justice Alito emphasize, the relevant inquiry is whether the State is the real party in interest, with treasury exposure and pervasive control serving as the most reliable proxies for the sovereignty and dignity concerns that animate the plan of the Convention. Nothing in New Jersey’s Tort Claims Act supplies the unmistakably clear, forum-specific consent necessary to subject the State (or its alter ego) to private damages suits in a sister State’s courts. Adopting a “commercial enterprise” carveout would invite precisely the kind of atextual, policy-driven erosion of interstate sovereign immunity that Hyatt and Alden foreclose absent a demonstrated surrender at the Founding.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point remains that NJ Transit’s separate corporate form and revenue-generating operations make it look like a commercial actor that should be suable like a public corporation. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, our arm-of-the-State inquiry—especially under Hess—cannot sensibly turn on an elastic “commercial activity” label without inviting the very ad hoc, policy-driven immunity determinations that undermine administrability and the federal balance; the more constitutionally grounded proxy is whether the State is the real party in interest through fiscal exposure and pervasive control. On this record, those indicia point strongly toward New Jersey itself, so a damages judgment would in substance run against a coequal sovereign, triggering Hyatt’s structural bar absent clear consent. And I agree with Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch that New Jersey’s tort-claims scheme does not supply the unmistakable, forum-specific waiver necessary to subject the State (or its alter ego) to private suit in a sister State’s courts.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest point is that NJ Transit’s separate incorporation and fare-charging, revenue-generating operations make it look like a market actor, such that treating it as the State risks letting States “launder” immunity through public corporations. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasized, our doctrine does not turn on a free-floating “commercial activity” label; it turns on whether the State is, in law and practical effect, the real party in interest—especially where the State’s control and the State fisc’s exposure to judgments are implicated. On this record, those indicia point toward New Jersey’s identification of NJ Transit with itself, and nothing in New Jersey’s tort-claims scheme supplies the unmistakably clear, forum-specific consent that would be required to subject the State (or its alter ego) to private damages litigation in a sister-State court. I therefore see no doctrinally grounded exception or waiver that displaces the baseline immunity rule recognized in Hyatt and related cases.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point is that NJ Transit’s separate corporate form and fare-charging operations make it look “commercial,” and that treating it as the State risks letting States launder immunity through public corporations. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Alito stressed, our arm-of-the-State cases—especially Hess—reject that free-form label in favor of the more constitutionally grounded question whether the State is the real party in interest, with the State’s legal/practical responsibility for judgments and control serving as the central proxies. And Petitioner’s waiver fallback cannot get off the ground: as Justice Gorsuch explained, nothing in New Jersey’s tort-claims framework supplies the unmistakably clear, forum-specific consent necessary to subject a State (or its alter ego) to private damages suits in another State’s courts. I therefore see no doctrinally recognized basis to depart from the default rule of interstate sovereign immunity here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point is the separate corporate form and ostensibly “commercial” operation, warning that States might launder immunity through public corporations. But that reframes the inquiry away from the Constitution’s structural immunity recognized in Hyatt and Alden: the question is whether New Jersey is the real party in interest and whether it has unmistakably consented to be haled into a sister State’s court. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the most administrable proxy consistent with our cases is the State’s legal and practical responsibility for judgments coupled with pervasive state control, and those indicia point toward NJ Transit as an arm of the State here. And I agree with Justice Alito that nothing in New Jersey’s tort-claims scheme supplies the clear, forum-specific waiver necessary to surrender a personal-jurisdiction-like structural immunity in another sovereign’s tribunal.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The strongest point for Petitioner is the “commercial marketplace” framing—NJ Transit sells tickets, is separately incorporated, and looks like a business—so treating it as the State might let States immunize revenue-generating entities by corporate design. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasized, our arm-of-the-State analysis does not turn on that commercial label; it turns on whether the State is the real party in interest, with state control and treasury exposure serving as the most administrable proxies (Hess). On this record, those indicia point to New Jersey, and nothing in New Jersey’s tort-claims scheme supplies the unmistakably clear, forum-specific consent to private damages suits in a sister-State court that Justice Gorsuch correctly stresses is required to overcome the default structural immunity. I would therefore resolve this case narrowly on these features—state integration, fiscal/dignitary consequences, and no clear extraterritorial waiver—without announcing any broader rule for all state-run transportation entities.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest contention—that NJ Transit’s separate corporate form and fare-charging, market-facing operations make it too “commercial” to share New Jersey’s immunity—would require us to recognize an atextual commercial-activity exception to interstate sovereign immunity. As Justice Kagan stressed, Hess directs us to the more constitutionally grounded proxy: whether the State is the real party in interest, especially given legal and practical exposure of the state fisc and the State’s control over the entity. Chief Justice Roberts is also right that this is not a backdoor waiver case: New Jersey’s tort-claims scheme may permit some suits in its own courts, but it lacks the unmistakably clear, forum-specific consent needed to subject the State (or its alter ego) to private damages actions in a sister-State tribunal. Absent textual, structural, or historical support for treating this Commerce-adjacent “commercial” instrumentality as special, precedent points to immunity here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest contention—that NJ Transit’s separate corporate form and fare-charging operations render it a “commercial” actor outside the State’s structural immunity—does not supply a workable doctrinal limiter and, as Justice Kagan noted, conflicts with Hess’s emphasis on whether the State is the real party in interest, particularly through fiscal responsibility and state control. On this record, the features colleagues highlighted (especially Chief Justice Roberts’s framing and Justice Alito’s focus on administrability) point to NJ Transit’s integration into New Jersey’s governance such that a damages judgment would, in practical operation, run against the State and implicate the dignity and fisc interests that drive Hyatt/Alden. Nor can New Jersey’s tort-claims scheme be converted into an out-of-state consent to private damages suits without the unmistakably clear, forum-specific statement our clear-statement cases require; inferring extraterritorial waiver would expand a jurisdictional waiver beyond what its text and place in the statutory structure support. The “commercial enterprise” label thus functions as an atextual exception that would destabilize the arm-of-the-State inquiry rather than anchor it in the structural question our precedents demand.

John Roberts.reasoning: Properly framed, this is not a waiver or abrogation case—so the “unmistakably clear” clear-statement rule does not do the work Petitioner wants—and the question is instead whether NJ Transit is so identified with New Jersey that treating it as suable like a private actor would subject the State itself to the indignity and practical burdens sovereign immunity is meant to prevent under the plan of the Convention. On the specific facts, NJ Transit is created by state law to perform a quintessential statewide governmental function, is subject to substantial state control in governance and operations, and New Jersey law treats it as part of the State’s governmental structure rather than as a municipal-style corporation; those features align this entity with the State for structural-immunity purposes, including in sister-state courts after Hyatt. While formal treasury liability is not the only consideration, it remains the central proxy for whether the suit is, in substance, against the State, and nothing in the record indicates a state-law consent to out-of-state litigation akin to a clear waiver. A rule minimizing those state-identification factors would be difficult to administer and would invite forum-shopping against state instrumentalities engaged in core public transportation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: State sovereign immunity is a structural incident of statehood retained in the plan of the Convention, including immunity from private suits in sister-State courts absent an unmistakable surrender or clear consent. The arm-of-the-State inquiry should therefore focus on whether New Jersey has made NJ Transit part of its governmental apparatus such that a private judgment would, as a practical and legal matter, operate against the State itself—an inquiry in which the State’s legal responsibility for judgments and its pervasive control are central because they implicate the State’s dignity and fiscal integrity. On these facts, where New Jersey law treats NJ Transit as an instrumentality of state government and there is no unequivocal waiver consenting to out-of-state private suits (the Tort Claims Act at most authorizes limited in-forum litigation), NJ Transit shares the State’s immunity. A multi-factor test cannot be used to dilute that retained immunity based on functional “commercial” labels when the State has not clearly surrendered immunity for this entity in the constitutional design or by explicit waiver.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Interstate sovereign immunity recognized in Hyatt rests on the Constitution’s structural commitment to the equality and dignity of the States, and that protection would be undermined if sister-State courts could hale an entity that is functionally part of New Jersey’s government into private damages litigation based on ad hoc, multi-factor balancing. In the arm-of-the-state analysis, Hess properly gives primacy to whether the State is legally and practically responsible for the entity’s debts and judgments, because that factor most directly implicates the sovereign treasury and the State’s retained sovereignty—here, New Jersey’s institutional design and asserted fiscal responsibility for NJ Transit point strongly toward treating it as the State for immunity purposes. Giving dispositive (or near-dispositive) weight to treasury risk also supplies the administrable, uniform rule that sovereign-immunity doctrine requires, rather than inviting inconsistent, politically inflected determinations about whether a public transportation enterprise is “commercial” enough to be sued. And absent a clear, express waiver, New Jersey’s tort-claims framework cannot be stretched into consent to private suits in another State’s courts.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: State sovereign immunity is the baseline rule, and it is displaced only by an unequivocal waiver or a clearly applicable exception; neither is present here because New Jersey’s tort-claims framework does not clearly consent to private suits against New Jersey (or its alter egos) in another State’s courts. On the arm-of-the-State question, the inquiry must remain functional and doctrine-driven, but the most important consideration is whether the State is legally or practically responsible for the entity’s debts and judgments—because that treasury risk is central to the immunity doctrine’s purposes of preserving state sovereignty and intergovernmental comity. On this record, NJ Transit’s structure and the State’s fiscal exposure and control make it sufficiently an alter ego of New Jersey to share the State’s immunity, and we should not infer a broader consent to out-of-state litigation from general operational “commercial” features. Accordingly, NJ Transit is entitled to immunity from these private suits absent a clear, express waiver extending to sister-State fora.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Our sovereign-immunity doctrine sets a clear baseline: absent consent, a State and its arms are not amenable to private suit, including in another State’s courts once arm-of-the-State status is established. Applying the arm-of-the-State inquiry as this Court has framed it, the dispositive consideration is the immunity doctrine’s core purpose of protecting the State’s dignity and treasury—so where New Jersey has structured NJ Transit such that the State bears the real legal and fiscal risk of judgments and treats the entity as part of state government rather than a municipal corporation, NJ Transit shares the State’s immunity. Petitioners’ effort to dilute that treasury-and-control focus in favor of a more freewheeling “commercial enterprise” label would require narrowing what our cases—most notably Hess—have said without qualification about the primacy of state financial liability. And nothing in the New Jersey Tort Claims Act or related state-law provisions amounts to the kind of unequivocal, out-of-state waiver of immunity that our precedents require.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: This case triggers the Constitution’s structural sovereign-immunity framework (Hyatt/Alden/Seminole Tribe), not the Eleventh Amendment’s rare, text-bound Article III bar, because the asserted protection is the State’s retained dignity and immunity from private suit in another sovereign’s tribunal and it operates like a personal-jurisdiction privilege that may be waived only by clear consent. On the arm-of-the-State question, the “most important” indicator is whether the State is legally responsible for the entity’s debts and judgments, since that is the practical measure of whether the suit is “in effect” against the State itself; here New Jersey’s fiscal responsibility and the State’s design and control over NJ Transit strongly indicate the real party in interest is the State. Other functional considerations (commercial operations, separate corporate form) may inform the inquiry, but they cannot overcome a showing that New Jersey remains on the hook and has structured NJ Transit to function as a governmental instrumentality. And nothing in the New Jersey Tort Claims Act supplies the sort of clear, express consent necessary to waive structural immunity in out-of-state or federal forums.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The starting point is the governing sovereign-immunity doctrine’s text and structure: state sovereign immunity is a constitutional background rule, and a State does not lightly surrender it absent a clear waiver. Applying the Court’s arm-of-the-state precedents, the most salient inquiry is whether a damages judgment would in law and practical operation implicate the State’s fisc, because that concern lies at the core of the Eleventh Amendment’s structural purpose. On this record, New Jersey has structured NJ Transit as a state instrumentality with substantial state control and a close financial relationship to the State, and there is no clear, express consent in the New Jersey Tort Claims Act (or elsewhere) to be sued in sister-state or federal courts. Given the mixed signals that often attend “commercial” state entities, the treasury/sovereign-responsibility factor and the clear-statement rule against implied waiver together tip the case to treating NJ Transit as an arm of the State entitled to immunity here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: A straightforward application of our arm-of-the-State precedents points toward treating NJ Transit as sharing New Jersey’s sovereign immunity, because the doctrine turns on structural limits protecting the State from being haled into private damages actions without consent. Under Hess and later cases, the “most important factor” is whether the State is legally or practically responsible for judgments; New Jersey’s institutional design and its treatment of NJ Transit as part of state government, together with the asserted exposure of the state fisc, weigh heavily in favor of arm-of-the-State status. Petitioners’ functional and policy-based arguments for diluting that factor cannot override the settled rule that sovereign immunity is a threshold constitutional protection, not an efficiency calculus, and state tort-claims provisions do not clearly waive immunity in sister-state (or federal) courts absent unmistakable consent. On remand, lower courts may consider the remaining state-law control and characterization factors, but nothing in the text, structure, or our precedents supports carving out a “commercial enterprise” exception that would deny immunity where the treasury-risk and state-control indicia point the other way.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: State sovereign immunity is the baseline, and an entity shares that immunity when the State’s law, institutional design, and practical operation show it functions as an arm of the State rather than as a separate municipal-style corporation. Here, the most structurally salient consideration is the State’s financial responsibility for judgments and the entity’s placement within New Jersey’s governmental architecture—features that, under this Court’s arm-of-the-state cases, strongly indicate that a suit is effectively against the State itself. While the inquiry remains multi-factor (including State control and the State’s expressed intent), giving dispositive weight to formal “labels” is unnecessary because the fiscal/structural alignment and State oversight, as presented, point in the same direction. And there is no unmistakably clear waiver or consent by New Jersey to private suits against NJ Transit in other jurisdictions (state tort-claims provisions, absent clear extraterritorial consent, do not suffice), so immunity applies.
